In his delivery-time regression project, he used Recursive Feature Elimination to cut 12 features down to 8, which dropped the test R² from 0.8800 to 0.8191, making the model measurably worse without him noticing at the time.
In that same project, he misattributed a six-point R² change to feature scaling when OLS is scale-invariant, and he left the unexplained gap sitting in his notebook for a year.

In his New York taxi exploratory data analysis, three figures were plotted from random numbers provided as starter-template scaffolding rather than real trip records, which scaled up noise and forced him to withdraw those conclusions.
In that taxi analysis, two conclusion cells contradicted each other on peak hours, and he left them unreconciled because he wrote them from impression rather than from the plots.

In his delivery-time and taxi projects, he wrote prose descriptions and conclusions that either described a completely different retail dataset or sat unverified inside triple-quoted strings in code cells where they never rendered as text.
For his internal Active Directory Python tool at Capgemini, he never wrote documentation, onboarded a second user, or handed it over, meaning its value ended entirely on his last day.

For that same access request tool, he never logged his approval decisions against the model's proposals to measure its acceptance rate or error patterns, failing to build an evidence base for whether it could run unattended.
